blocks.label: Not at all / not much
blocks.rationale: The negative-degree scale: each sets how strong a 'no' is before a negative verb or adjective, from zenzen 'not at all' to sonna ni 'not that much'. nakanaka adds 'just won't', for things that are slow or hard to make happen.
blocks.interference: zenzen means 'not at all', hotondo 'hardly' and anmari 'not very'. sonna ni ('not that …') measures against a degree already in the air, either what someone said or what you'd expect, so it often answers a worry or a claim; anmari just rates the thing as low. nakanaka is about time and effort, not amount: nakanaka konai = it's taking ages, zenzen konai = it isn't coming at all. Without a negative, hotondo flips to 'almost all', sonna ni to 'so much' and nakanaka to 'pretty, more than expected' (nakanaka ii is close to kekkou ii but sounds like a verdict).

items.use: With a negative it means something just won't happen despite trying or waiting, or is taking ages (nakanaka konai, nakanaka oboerarenai, nakanaka umaku ikanai). Before an adjective it means 'pretty, more than expected' (nakanaka ii, nakanaka muzukashii).

example.ja: バス、なかなか来ないね
example.english: The bus is taking forever, huh.

examplePolite.ja: バス、なかなか来ませんね
examplePolite.english: The bus is taking a while, isn't it.

items.freqNote: kana spelling; rank covers both senses (中々 is #54755)
items.notes: Used as praise, it sounds like you're grading the thing. To a boss, or to the person who cooked, say hontou ni or sugoku instead.

changelog.change: Moved from B2 to B5 (Not at all / not much, now 5 items) because it was re-added for its 'just won't' sense, which sits beside zenzen. B2 stays exactly as it was.

Rewrote the B5 rationale and interference for the merged block. The old content is kept, and they now add the nakanaka konai vs zenzen konai trap and nakanaka's flip without a negative (close to kekkou ii).
contrastGroup changed from null to zenzen-anmari-hotondo.
use now covers the 'despite trying or waiting' sense (nakanaka oboerarenai) and describes the positive sense as a degree adverb before any adjective (nakanaka muzukashii), not only nakanaka ii.
Example glosses now read 'taking forever' / 'taking a while' so they don't suggest 'never coming' or 'not coming at all'.

english reordered to lead with the negative sense, '(not) easily; just won't; quite'. freqNote now gives the 中々 rank (#54755). Re-checked: #494 is from tool output, and the core-vocab pointer is correct.

blocks.label: Getting through, giving up, not wasting a chance
blocks.rationale: Words for handling a situation: start somewhere, push past the details, manage somehow, say how it ended, take an outcome as settled in advance, and don't waste a chance or an effort.
blocks.interference: toriaezu (for now, as a first step) and tonikaku (anyway, whatever else) share '___ yatte miyou'. nantoka is about managing despite trouble; kekkyoku is about the final outcome. douse also comes out as 'anyway', but tonikaku pushes on while douse takes the outcome as settled in advance, usually the bad one (douse muri da, it won't work anyway); kekkyoku reports how it really ended (kekkyoku muri datta). sekkaku can't fill the '___ yatte miyou' slot on its own. It needs da kara: sekkaku da kara yatte miyou (since we have the chance), never 'sekkaku yatte miyou'. douse nara (if it's happening anyway) gives 'might as well': douse matsu nara, kafe de matou (if we have to wait anyway, let's wait in a café). It starts from 'this is happening regardless', where sekkaku starts from 'this is a rare chance'. sekkaku ... noni (after all that trouble) often leads into kekkyoku: sekkaku tsukutta noni, kekkyoku tabenakatta (I went to the trouble of making it, and in the end they didn't eat it).

items.english: anyway (it's settled regardless); might as well (douse nara)
items.use: Treats an outcome as settled whatever you do. Often it's resigned (douse muri da, douse wasureru yo), and aimed at someone it sounds sulky or bitter (douse kikanai n desho). It's also a neutral 'anyway' when you give a reason: douse hima da shi, tetsudau yo (I'm free anyway, so I'll help). It never moves a story on the way English 'anyway' does; that's tonikaku.

example.english: It's not going to work anyway.

examplePolite.english: It's not going to work anyway.

items.freqNote: どうせ #580; どうせなら #5798 counted separately
items.notes: douse nara (if it's happening anyway) is the upbeat 'might as well': douse nara ii no kaou yo (if we're buying one anyway, let's get a good one).

changelog.change: english: replaced 'anyway (resigned); it's hopeless' with 'anyway (it's settled regardless); might as well (douse nara)'. 'it's hopeless' is what douse muri da means, not douse on its own (all 3 reviews; nuance rated it major).

use: now says douse treats an outcome as settled, usually with resignation and sulky when aimed at someone. Added the neutral reason use (douse hima da shi, tetsudau yo) and a warning that it never moves a story on the way English 'anyway' does (that's tonikaku). Moved douse nara out to notes (natural + nuance).
notes: now introduces douse nara directly as the upbeat 'might as well', with the example kept (nuance).
prereqs: added E-nara for the douse nara pattern, matching how sekkaku lists its pattern prereqs. Checked that E-nara exists in the list (nuance).

C7 interference: added the douse vs tonikaku 'anyway' trap (major, nuance). Widened 'looks ahead and expects the worst' to 'takes the outcome as settled in advance, usually the bad one'. 'that slot' now reads 'the ___ yatte miyou slot' so it points at the right frame. Replaced the confusing 'douse nara yatte miyou also means might as well' with a concrete example: douse matsu nara, kafe de matou (natural + form + nuance).
C7 label: 'Getting through, not wasting a chance' -> 'Getting through, giving up, not wasting a chance' so it covers douse (natural).
C7 rationale: 'shrug at an outcome you can't change' -> 'take an outcome as settled in advance'. This covers both the resigned and the neutral uses (nuance wording, over natural's 'write off').

blocks.label: Like & dislike
blocks.rationale: The ways to say how you feel about a thing, from love and like through 'not my thing' to dislike and can't stand; all take the X ga ___ frame.
blocks.interference: kirai is a settled dislike of a thing or person; iya is a gut rejection, 'I don't want this / this is unpleasant', usually about what is happening now. Drill 'ame no hi, kirai' (rainy days in general) against 'mata ame? iya da naa' (the rain today). iya also sounds like the interjection iya ('no / well', G): the interjection is soft and opens a reply (iya, chigau yo), while the adjective is emphatic and stands alone or ends the sentence (iya!, iya da, iya na yokan). daisuki is just a stronger suki (dai- = big) on the same rainy-days sentence, so add it once suki is solid. nigate is the soft kirai on that same sentence (ame no hi, nigate = rainy days aren't my thing) and the safe choice about food or people, so add it after kirai. It also means 'bad at' about yourself (eigo ga nigate); its opposite is tokui (my strong point), while jouzu (good at, later block) is praise for someone else.

items.use: Says something isn't your thing: a food, a type of person, or a task you're weak at (X ga nigate). It is softer and safer than kirai, and it is the modest way to say you're bad at something (eigo ga nigate).

example.english: Rainy days aren't really my thing.

examplePolite.romaji: ame no hi ga nigate desu
examplePolite.english: Rainy days aren't really my thing.

items.notes: The opposite is tokui (my strong point). heta (bad at) is fine about yourself but blunt about other people, and nigate also hints you don't enjoy it. Don't mix it up with nigai (bitter): koohii, nigate = I'm not into coffee; koohii, nigai = the coffee's bitter.

blocks.label: Glad, let down, worried
blocks.rationale: Your own emotional reactions to news, to what's coming and to being noticed: glad, disappointed, looking forward, scared, worried, embarrassed.
blocks.interference: kowai (scared) and shinpai (worried) share the exam-results sentence so only the feeling changes, and ureshii and zannen are paired replies to news. kowai also sounds like kawaii (cute, earlier block): three beats against four. tanoshimi (looking forward to it) is not tanoshii (fun, earlier block): say ryokou, tanoshimi before the trip and ryokou, tanoshikatta after it. hazukashii (embarrassed, shy) and ureshii are the two ways to take a compliment, bashful against pleased. hazukashii is one beat away from muzukashii (difficult, earlier block): ha-zu-ka-shii vs mu-zu-ka-shii, so add it once muzukashii is solid, then drill chotto hazukashii against chotto muzukashii and listen for ha- vs mu-.

items.use: Says you feel embarrassed or shy, or that something is embarrassing: after a mistake, at a compliment or when being watched ('hazukashii!', hazukashii kara yamete = stop, it's embarrassing).

example.ja: ちょっと恥ずかしいな

examplePolite.ja: ちょっと恥ずかしいです

items.notes: About someone else or what they did, it is a criticism ('embarrassing, shameful'). For how someone else feels, say hazukashisou (looks embarrassed).

blocks.label: Size, length & amount
blocks.rationale: How big or long something is and how much of it there is: the size and quantity scales, plus nagai for length and for time.
blocks.interference: ookii (big) and ooi (many) both start with oo-: hito ga ooi means 'crowded', while ookii hito is 'a big person'. Within each pair, learn the first word before adding its opposite. nagai is length and duration (kami ga nagai, nagai aida = a long time), not overall size, and it shares ookii's 'kono X, chotto ___' sentence. For a long way (distance) say tooi (far), not nagai: eki made tooi.

items.use: Describes length (hair, lines, roads) and, just as often, duration: a long film, meeting or wait. nagai aida means 'for a long time'.

example.ja: この映画、ちょっと長いね
example.english: This film's a bit long, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kono eiga wa chotto nagai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この映画はちょっと長いですね
examplePolite.english: This film is a little long, isn't it?

items.notes: nagaku natte gomen = sorry this got long (a message or a talk); the opposite is mijikai (short).

blocks.label: Hot, cold, ouch, look out
blocks.rationale: How the weather and your body feel, and when something is dangerous: hot, cold, it hurts and watch out. These are the daily small-talk openers and the reports and warnings you have to make on the spot.
blocks.interference: atsui and samui are opposites with the same shape (three beats ending -ui) on the same sentence (kyou, ___ ne), so learn atsui first; per 11-list-adjectives note 9(a), keep samui at least 10 items after atsui in drill order even though they share a block. atsui covers hot air and hot things, but samui is only for the air and how you feel: a cold drink is tsumetai. itai (it hurts) sounds almost the same as iru + -tai (want to stay): atama ga itai vs zutto koko ni itai, and the words before it tell you which. abunai is the warning about the situation, while kowai (scared, later block) is the feeling: shout abunai! to stop someone. abunai ends in -nai but is not a negative (not dangerous = abunakunai), so per 11-list-adjectives #42 add it only once the -kunai negative is solid. As reflex shouts all four clip to the stem: atsu!, samu!, ita!, abuna!

items.use: Warns of danger on the spot (abunai! = watch out!) and calls anything risky, from a road to a plan. It also says something is at risk (jikan, abunai = we might not make it; tesuto, abunai = I might fail). After a near miss, abunakatta = that was close.

example.romaji: soko, abunai yo! ki o tsukete
example.ja: そこ、危ないよ！気をつけて

examplePolite.romaji: soko, abunai desu yo. ki o tsukete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: そこ、危ないですよ。気をつけてください
examplePolite.english: It's dangerous there. Please be careful.

items.notes: As a shout, abunai! is fine to anyone, strangers included, with no desu; abunee! is the rough, mostly male version. 'Not dangerous' is abunakunai.

changelog.change: D9 interference (major, natural + nuance): replaced the weak 'ha-zu-ka-shii vs u-re-shii' sound note with the real near-twin muzukashii (earlier block, one beat apart). Learn it after muzukashii, then drill chotto hazukashii against chotto muzukashii. Kept the compliment sentence.
prereqs: added D-muzukashii to match the new drill-order guard.
notes (nuance): about someone else it is a criticism ('shameful'); for another person's feelings say hazukashisou.

D2 interference (all three reviews): no longer pairs nigate with jouzu as opposites. The opposite is now tokui, jouzu is described as praise for others, and '(D13)' became 'later block' to match house style.
notes (natural + nuance): heta is fine about yourself but blunt about others, and nigate hints at not enjoying it. Added the nigai (bitter) ear trap with a coffee pair.

D10 interference (nuance + form): swapped the 'tall person = se ga takai (D8)' sentence for the real English-transfer error, a long way = tooi (eki made tooi), which also removes the block-ID reference.
alsoIn: exit-battery pointer is now '13-list-exit-battery #29 (in example)'.

use (nuance): added the at-risk sense (jikan, abunai; tesuto, abunai) and kept abunakatta for a near miss.

D12 interference (form + natural + nuance): 'kowai (D9)' -> 'kowai (scared, later block)'. Added a drill-order guard: abunai is not a negative, so per 11-list-adjectives #42 add it only once the -kunai negative is solid.

blocks.label: Depends / without / instead / for / so that
blocks.rationale: Linkers that do the job of an English preposition or 'so that': depends on X, without doing X, instead of X, in order to / for X, so that (not) X.
blocks.interference: -naide (without) vs -nakute (because not). -naide and -kawari ni both come out as 'instead of': -naide follows verbs only and also means 'without' (kasa motanaide deta, where kawari ni can't go), while kawari ni also follows nouns (koohii no kawari ni ocha) and can mean 'in return' (oshiete kureru kawari ni ogoru; sentence-initial sono kawari = 'but in return'). -tame ni (purpose, an action you choose) vs -you ni (so that): after potentials and verbs you don't control only you ni sounds right (hanaseru you ni, maniau you ni, not hanaseru tame ni); after -nai, you ni is the everyday choice (wasurenai you ni) and -nai tame ni sounds stiff. Listen around it: noun + no you ni is 'like' (yume no you ni), itta you ni is 'like I said', and you ni naru / you ni iu mean 'come to' / 'tell someone to'; they all sound the same.

items.use: Puts one thing in place of another: noun + no kawari ni = 'instead of X' (koohii no kawari ni ocha), plain verb + kawari ni = 'instead of doing' or 'in return for doing' (oshiete kureru kawari ni, ogoru yo = teach me and I'll buy you dinner). At the start of a sentence sono kawari (no ni) sets a condition, 'but in return' (ii yo. sono kawari, ashita tetsudatte ne), or balances a downside, 'to make up for it' (takai kedo, sono kawari oishii).

example.romaji: watashi no kawari ni itte kureru?
example.ja: 私の代わりに行ってくれる？
example.english: Can you go in my place?

examplePolite.romaji: watashi no kawari ni itte kuremasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 私の代わりに行ってくれませんか？
examplePolite.english: Could you go in my place?

items.freqNote: 代わりに #1457 (exact form); bare noun 代わり #870 and その代わり #2876 are separate entries; homophone 変わる #226
items.notes: Same sound as kawaru 'change' (H-kawaru) and its noun kawari (kawari nai? = how've you been?), but this kawari comes from the other kawaru, 'take someone's place' (kawarou ka? = want me to take over?). Said alone, kawari ni = 'instead' (kawari ni yattoku yo = I'll do it instead); kawari alone = a replacement (kawari ga inai). okawari = seconds / a refill. Even in polite speech the verb before it stays plain: iku kawari ni denwa shimashita, not ikimasu kawari ni.

blocks.label: How sure
blocks.rationale: A ladder of certainty from 'maybe' through 'should be' to 'no way', all on one base sentence about someone arriving.
blocks.interference: From least to most sure: kamo (could go either way), to omou (my opinion), n ja nai (I'd guess), hazu (should, by reasoning); wake nai is just as sure in the other direction (no way). hazu is about what you expect: not your own plans, which take tsumori, and never advice, which takes -ta hou ga ii. hazu ga nai also means 'can't be', but calmly, by reasoning; wake nai is the everyday, emphatic one. wake nai and wake ja nai both deny, but one ja softens it: kirai na wake nai = no way I'd hate it, kirai na wake ja nai (kedo) = it's not that I hate it (but...).

items.use: Flatly rules something out as impossible or absurd ('no way', 'as if'). On its own it makes the stock retort sonna wake nai (jan)! = no way / that can't be. It goes on any plain clause, often with jan or desho (wakaru wake nai jan = how would I know?), and nouns and na-adjectives take na before it (uso na wake nai, hima na wake nai).

example.english: No way they'll be here yet.

examplePolite.romaji: mada tsuku wake nai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: まだ着くわけないですよ
examplePolite.english: There's no way they'll be here yet.

items.freqNote: わけない #449 (token also covers the adjective 訳ない 'easy', whose kanji spelling is #8290); わけがない #2398; cf. はずない #2095, はずがない #2504
items.notes: One ja softens it rather than flipping it: kirai na wake ja nai (kedo) = it's not that I hate it (but...). The same word is also an adjective meaning 'easy, no trouble': sonna no wake nai yo = that's nothing, one 'no' away from sonna wake nai yo = no way. Even in polite speech it flatly contradicts, so don't aim it at a superior's idea (say sore wa chotto... instead). The careful polite form is wake ga arimasen.

changelog.change: Dropped the leading hyphen and 〜 (romaji 'wake nai', ja/kana 'わけない') so it matches hazu, kamo and wake da, which are free clause-final words (all three reviews).

Polite form changed from 'wake ga nai desu' to 'wake nai desu' / わけないです, the everyday spoken form and parallel to the casual one (native-naturalness view wins on wording). examplePolite is now 'mada tsuku wake nai desu yo' / まだ着くわけないですよ. The careful form 'wake ga arimasen' moved to notes.

F6 interference: removed the false claim that wake nai is the 'opposite' of wake ja nai (major). Both deny, and ja only softens a flat denial into a partial one. Added how it differs from hazu ga nai (calm, reasoned) and kept the old F6 text.
use: added the stock retort 'sonna wake nai (jan)!' and a noun example (uso na wake nai).

notes: 'ja flips it' became 'ja softens it'. Added the trap with 訳ない 'easy' (sonna no wake nai yo = that's nothing), the warning not to aim it at a superior's idea, and the careful polite form wake ga arimasen.

freqNote: re-checked with the tool (わけない #449, 訳ない #8290, わけがない #2398, はずない #2095, はずがない #2504). It now says the #449 token also counts the 'easy' adjective, and はずない is added as the fairer comparison.

blocks.label: Hello and goodbye
blocks.rationale: Fixed greetings for the time of day, first meetings, phone calls and leaving.
blocks.interference: hajimemashite opens a first meeting and yoroshiku closes it. konnichiwa is for people you aren't close to; with friends, say ohayou in the morning and otherwise just start talking. moshimoshi is the hello for phone and video calls, not for greeting someone in person.

items.use: Opens a phone or video call, and checks the line when the other person goes quiet or the sound cuts out; it isn't used to greet someone in person.

examplePolite.ja: もしもし、今大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: Hello, is now a good time?

items.notes: Checking the line: moshimoshi? kikoeru? (hello? can you hear me?). When you answer a work phone, say hai, [name] desu rather than moshimoshi. Face to face it's either a joking 'hello? anyone home?' or an older speaker's 'excuse me' to a stranger.

blocks.label: Surprise
blocks.rationale: Quick reactions to the unexpected, from puzzlement to disbelief, plus bikkuri shita to say something surprised you.
blocks.interference: e? reacts to something you just heard, while are? reacts to something you notice. honto? asks whether it's true, while uso! exclaims that it can't be. bikkuri shita says it surprised you (or made you jump), so you can also use it later when you tell someone about it.

items.english: that surprised me; you startled me
items.use: The everyday way to say something surprised you, whether it's news you heard or someone making you jump. It works in the moment and also when you tell the story later.

example.romaji: kekkon suru tte kiite, bikkuri shita yo.
example.ja: 結婚するって聞いて、びっくりしたよ。
example.english: I was surprised to hear you're getting married.

examplePolite.romaji: kekkon suru tte kiite, bikkuri shimashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: 結婚するって聞いて、びっくりしましたよ。
examplePolite.english: I was surprised to hear you're getting married.

items.freqNote: びっくりした #1488; びっくり #1350
items.notes: Like yokatta, it stays past even in the moment. After a jump scare you say aa, bikkuri shita! (you scared me!). The non-past bikkuri suru looks ahead: bikkuri suru yo (you'll be surprised). Mark what surprised you with ni: sono nyuusu ni bikkuri shita.

blocks.label: Phrases for occasions
blocks.rationale: Fixed phrases tied to a particular moment: meals, bedtime, the end of shared work, someone heading out, and seeing someone again.
blocks.interference: itadakimasu comes before eating and gochisousama after. oyasumi, otsukare and ki o tsukete are all sign-offs: oyasumi for the night, otsukare after work or study together, and ki o tsukete as someone heads out (it also works as a warning: 'careful!'). hisashiburi greets someone you're meeting again and is never a goodbye.

items.use: Said to anyone heading off (going home at night, driving, on a trip), and as a warning ('careful!'). Adding ne (ki o tsukete ne) makes it warmer.

example.romaji: jaa, mata ashita. ki o tsukete ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、また明日。気をつけてね。
example.english: Okay, see you tomorrow. Take care.

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, mata ashita. ki o tsukete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、また明日。気をつけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Well, see you tomorrow. Please take care.

items.freqNote: 気をつけて #1735 (気を付けて #2563 counted separately); verb 気をつける #1226
items.notes: You learn this one as a set phrase. The verb ki o tsukeru comes later (H-ki-o-tsukeru) and adds ki o tsukete kaette ne (get home safe) and ki o tsukemasu (I'll be careful). As a warning it's often shouted on its own: abunai, ki o tsukete! To see off a customer or a senior, say oki o tsukete (お気をつけて), often as oki o tsukete okaeri kudasai, because bare ki o tsukete kudasai sounds more like an instruction.

changelog.change: prereqs changed from [H-ki-o-tsukeru] to []. That prereq pointed forward from a stage-1 block (G13) to a stage-2 item (H8, #212), and like itadakimasu the phrase is learned as a chunk (major, all three reviews).

Notes rewritten so they point forward. The phrase comes first and the verb card comes later, adding ki o tsukete kaette ne and ki o tsukemasu. blocks.label: Take, put, cost, call, enough
blocks.rationale: Wide-reach light verbs whose meaning comes from the object: toru (take, pass, get), dasu (put out, take out, hand in, pay) and its opposite ireru (put in, include, make tea), kakaru (time or money it takes), kakeru (cause trouble, call, spend, put on), plus tariru for whether what you have is enough.
blocks.interference: 'It takes an hour' is kakaru, not toru; kakaru (it takes, ga) and kakeru (spend, call, o) are an intransitive/transitive pair: jikan ga kakaru vs jikan o kakeru. dasu is likewise the transitive partner of deru, and ireru of hairu: uchi o deta (I left home) vs gomi o dashita (I put the trash out), heya ni haitta (I went in) vs kaban ni ireta (I put it in the bag). kakaru says how much something takes and tariru whether you have that much (kekkou kakaru kedo, okane tariru?).

items.english: put in; include; make (tea); turn on
items.use: Puts something into something else, with the thing marked by o and the place by ni (kaban ni ireru); it also covers making tea or coffee, letting someone into a group or plan (watashi mo irete), and switching something on.

example.ja: コーヒーに砂糖入れる？
example.english: Do you take sugar in your coffee?

examplePolite.ja: コーヒーにお砂糖入れますか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like sugar in your coffee?

items.freqNote: 入れる #222; 淹れる (making tea/coffee) #19863 listed separately
items.notes: Ichidan (irete, ireta), unlike its godan partner hairu (haitte, haitta).

items.use: Says whether there's enough money, time, food or people, with the thing marked by ga; you mostly hear it as tarinai (not enough) and in the question tariru? (kore de tariru?).

examplePolite.ja: 時間が全然足りません。

items.freqNote: 足りる #764; 足りない #3974 separately (tokenizer mostly splits it into 足り + ない)
items.notes: Also means 'short of' or 'missing': hitori tarinai = we're one person short. 'That's enough!' / 'no more, thanks' is mou ii, not tariru.

blocks.label: Wrong, stuck, angry
blocks.rationale: Reactions when something's off: it's different or wrong, I'm in a bind, I made a mistake, someone's angry about it.
blocks.interference: chigau is a state (that's wrong / different) and machigaeru an act (I got it wrong): bangou chigau yo vs bangou machigaeta. okoru is also an act (getting angry), so 'she's angry' is okotteru and 'I got told off' is the passive okorareta; it sounds the same as okoru 'happen'.

items.use: Says someone gets angry: the person you're angry at takes ni (tomodachi ni okotta), and the person you tell off takes o (kodomo o okoru); 'is angry' right now is okotteru, and the passive okorareta means 'got told off'.

examplePolite.ja: まだ怒ってるんですか？

items.freqNote: 怒る #381; homophone 起こる (happen) #936 listed separately
items.notes: okoranaide = don't be mad; sugu okoru = gets angry easily. Homophone 起こる 'happen' is a separate verb.

blocks.label: Favours, passive, causative
blocks.rationale: The giving/receiving triad that marks who benefits from an action, the everyday thanks built on kureru, the passive for things done to you (often unwanted), and the causative in its everyday jobs: -sasete for asking to do something yourself, and -sasete morau / -sasete kureru for being allowed to.
blocks.interference: Same act, three viewpoints: tomodachi ga oshiete kureta / tomodachi ni oshiete moratta / tomodachi ni oshiete ageta. Kureru points toward the speaker, ageru away, and morau takes the receiver's view with the giver on ni. The passive keeps that ni frame, often for something unwanted: tomodachi ni tetsudatte moratta (glad) vs tomodachi ni okorareta (not glad), so a favour takes -te morau, not the passive. The ichidan passive sounds like the I3 potential (taberareru = can eat / gets eaten), while godan keeps them apart (ieru / iwareru); casual potentials often drop the ra (tabereru), passives never do. When you thank someone for an act, keep the kureru: oshiete kurete arigatou, never oshiete arigatou or oshiete agete arigatou. The causative swaps the passive's -are-/-rare- for -ase-/-sase- on the same stem (iwareta = I was told, iwasete = let me say), and -asete/-sasete asks to do it yourself where plain -te asks the other person: kangaete (you think it over) vs kangaesasete (let me think it over). Godan verbs never take the extra sa: yasumasete, not yasumasasete.

items.politeJa: 〜あせてください／〜させてください
items.use: Asks to be allowed to do something yourself: to have a go (yarasete, let me try), to offer (harawasete, let me pay) or to stall (chotto kangaesasete, let me think). Godan verbs change -u to -asete (yaru -> yarasete; after a vowel, -u becomes -wasete: harau -> harawasete), ichidan verbs swap -ru for -sasete (kangaeru -> kangaesasete), and the irregulars are sasete and kosasete.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は払わせてください。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; the tokenizer folds the causative into the verb (auxiliaries せる #16515, させる #31829); only lexicalised forms rank on their own (待たせる #851, やらせる #7775, 休ませる #27904; short -asu forms やらす #4504, 待たす #7648); 払わせる, 考えさせる, 言わせる not found
alsoIn: 05-acquisition-order contested calls, month 8 (causative productive only in -sasete kudasai / -sasete morau)
items.notes: The stalling set phrase is chotto kangaesasete (polite: sukoshi kangaesasete kudasai). Two more everyday frames to produce: with gomen it apologises for what you put someone through (matasete gomen, shinpai sasete gomen; polite matasete sumimasen), and with the favour verbs it reports permission (kyou wa hayaku kaerasete moratta, I got to go home early today; kaerasete kureta, they let me go home). Casual speech often shortens godan -asete to -ashite (yarashite, iwashite); recognise it, but produce -asete. Making someone do something in general (kodomo ni yasai o tabesaseru) is recognition-only for now.

blocks.label: How / this way
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/do manner words plus dou yatte, dou iu and dou shita: how something went, how it is done, 'like that', what exactly is going on, and what's wrong.
blocks.interference: dou asks for an opinion or report (dou datta?), dou yatte asks for the method (dou yatte iku?), dou iu koto? asks what's going on or what someone is getting at (once it's explained: aa, sou iu koto ka), and dou shita no? asks what has happened to you. dou iu asks what something is, donna (J7) what it is like: dou iu hito? = who is he to you, donna hito? = what's he like, and donna koto? = like what?; for what a word means, use dou iu imi? (G). The bare reply sou (sou da ne) is drilled in G, so the so- card here is sou iu.

items.english: what exactly (+ noun); dou iu koto? = how so? what's going on?
items.use: Goes before a noun to ask what exactly something is: dou iu koto? (how so? what's going on?), dou iu hito? (who is he, exactly? how do you know him?), dou iu kankei? (how are you two connected?). It is the question partner of sou iu. To ask what a word means, use dou iu imi? (G).

example.romaji: e, dou iu koto? ashita konai no?
example.ja: え、どういうこと？明日来ないの？
example.english: Wait, what's going on? You're not coming tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: e, dou iu koto desu ka? ashita konai n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: え、どういうことですか？明日来ないんですか？
examplePolite.english: Wait, what's going on? You're not coming tomorrow?

items.notes: dou iu koto? with a light rising tone is the everyday 'how so?'; said flat and hard it becomes 'what is the meaning of this?!', like dou iu wake? (see F-wake-da). With clerks and strangers, dou iu imi desu ka? (G) is the safe way to ask for clarification. In nihongo de dou iu? (how do you say it in Japanese?), iu is the verb 'say', not this word.
